name: Track competitor App Store listing changes with Bright Data, GPT-5.6, data tables and Slack

parameters.content:
## Watch what your competitors change on the App Store, not just when they ship

A store listing is positioning with a date on it. Subtitles get rewritten, prices move, screenshots get replaced, languages get added. None of it is announced.

### How it works

Paste App Store URLs into **Settings**. Bright Data returns the full listing for each one, and **`Find What Changed`** compares eleven fields against what was stored last run: version, price, in-app purchases, subtitle, the opening of the description, screenshot count, languages, size, rating, and the one-star and five-star shares.

The star distribution is there because the rating is not enough. All three apps used in testing show **4.8**; one of them carries three times the one-star share of the others. A rounded average hides exactly the thing you want to see.

Only apps that actually moved reach GPT-5.6, and it is given the old and new text rather than asked to remember. A week where nothing changed ends at **`Quiet Week`** with no message.

### Setup

1. Bright Data, as a Header Auth credential. The free tier is 5,000 credits a month with no card.

2. An OpenAI credential and a Slack credential.

3. A Data Table called `app_listings` with columns `app_id`, `title`, `version`, `price`, `sub_title`, `desc_head`, `desc_hash`, `screenshots`, `languages`, `rating`, `one_star` and `checked_at`.

4. The first run has nothing to compare against, so it records everything and reports nothing. Week two is when it starts working.

## 1. A list of rivals, pasted in
No sheet, no CRM. Fifteen App Store URLs in a Set node is the whole configuration, and the list is what a PMM already keeps in their head.

## 2. One job, however many apps
The Web Scraper API takes an array. Three listings came back in under twenty seconds, so there is no reason to split them.

## 3. Wait, but not forever
The poll cap lives in the Code node, because a Wait has no idea how many times it has run.

## 4. Flatten, and drop the wreckage
`include_errors=true` puts error rows in the snapshot. Five of thirty review rows in testing were nothing but an error message.

## 5. Eleven fields, compared to last week
Rating alone cannot separate three apps that all show 4.8. The one-star share can, so it is diffed with a threshold rather than ignored.

## 6. Only what moved costs a model call
The whole run collapses to one item first, so this is one decision rather than one per app. A quiet week ends here with no message.

## 7. One message, in the order it happened
The icons come from the field that moved, not from the model, so a price change reads as a price change every week.

## Reviews cannot tell you how a release landed

This deliberately does not read App Store reviews, and the reason is measured rather than stylistic. Review rows carry the app version **at the time the review was written** - Notion's reviews came back tagged 1.7.283 while the live listing said 1.7.331 - so filtering to the current release returns nothing at all. The newest review in a 25-row pull was six months old. Google Play review rows carry no version whatsoever.

Any workflow that claims to summarise reaction to a specific release from this data is reporting on last winter and calling it Thursday.

`number_of_raters` is rounded to the nearest thousand and the star shares are whole percentages, so small movements are invisible. Treat a one-point shift as a signal to go and look, not as a measurement.
